dispositions.method: The automatic families first printed in 1793 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running, families of 3 or more papers rather than the default 4, because 1793 has few papers in print), were split into single printed items (items.json: 10 items in 7 papers, none in 8 or more, 22 in exactly 6). The script was also run with year 1792 over the 1793 pages (items_from_1792.json); none of those items reaches 6 papers. Two AI reviewers (Claude Fable) read the items of each half of the year in 4 or more papers and proposed the stories; each item's printings were looked for with phrase searches over all 1,751 pages of 1793 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json), and every hit was read. Papers with pages in a story's weeks but no printing were searched with loose keywords. Every admitted printing was then checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points.json).
dispositions.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1807 and 1808: a story needs one printed item found in 7 or more newspapers, counted item by item. No item of 1793 reaches 8 papers; every non-digest item in 7 papers was admitted. Where several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story, and a sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent reaches 7 (the rule the owner agreed for 1776 round two): Dumouriez's address (6 papers), Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation of 5 April (5) and Jay and King's statement on Genet (5). The two titles of one renamed paper (the New-Hampshire Gazette at Portsmouth; Ranlet's paper at Exeter, the New Hampshire Gazetteer and then the American Herald of Liberty) were never counted twice toward a threshold; no admitted story's count depends on them. Both scanned copies of a Kentucky Gazette issue count once. A paper that printed an item again counts each printing. A 6-paper threshold for this year is proposed in the README and was not applied.

counted_item_by_item.Giles's resolutions on the Secretary of: The item finder counts 7 papers and 17 printings. The resolutions as moved are in GUS 2 Mar, NGz 6 Mar, MIR 18 Mar and NHGA 19 Mar, and as the House journal of 28 February and 1 March in NGz 3 and 6 Apr, NHG 23 Apr and AHL 14 May: 6 catalogue numbers but 5 papers, because NHGA and NHG are one paper. The Kentucky Gazette prints only the debate, in which speakers quote single resolutions; votes and speeches in GUS and NGz were not counted.
counted_item_by_item.Neighbouring paragraphs and chained item: The finder joins neighbouring paragraphs of a news column into chains: the Brussels paragraph of 17 October 1792 stands beside a Rome paragraph (6 papers) and a paragraph on the suttlers of Clairfayt's army (5); the Madeira paragraph is chained to the Philadelphia paragraphs after it in GUS. Each group here is the single item. Dumouriez's address was split by the finder into five items and Saxe-Cobourg's two proclamations into four; they are one document and two documents.
counted_item_by_item.Genet's letter and the answer: Genet's letter of 13 August and the Secretary of State's answer of 16 August were printed together in all seven papers. They are two signed documents, each its own group under a parent, with Jay and King's statement, which the letter answers, as a third group.
counted_item_by_item.Two settings of one paragraph: The Sun paragraph of 10 April is printed with a New York introduction ('In the Sun, of the 10th April, which is the latest paper received') in GUS, NGz (1 June), PG and NHG, and among London paragraphs in NGz (29 May), AHL, MIR and KG; the paragraph itself is the same and is counted as one item.
counted_item_by_item.Quotations: Pages that only quote or answer an item were not counted: Jay and King's statement quoted in NGz 24 Aug, 4 and 21 Sep and in their own later statement (PG 23 Dec), and commented on in PG 2 Sep and CI 28 Aug.

not_admitted.The 1793 news that no single item carrie: The execution of Louis XVI (six different accounts, none in more than 5 of the 6 papers then in print), France's decree of war on Britain and Holland (5), the French Republic's letter to the United States (5), Giles's resolutions (5 papers), the neutrality proclamation (4 papers by its own text), Washington's second inauguration (4), Genet's arrival and the addresses to him (2 to 4 each), the yellow fever in Philadelphia (no shared item above 4 papers), Toulon (no item above 4), the President's address of 3 December (4 papers, all those then in print) and the Algerine captures (Church's circular, 3).
not_admitted.Candidates in 6 papers: Proposed to the owner under a 6-paper threshold, not admitted: the list of the powers at war with France (two introductions, 3 + 3), the London Gazette bulletin from Tournai of 3 May, Hamilton's circular to the collectors with the President's rules on neutrality, the declaration of the President of the National Convention on a plot, the Cadiz letter of 24 June, the commissioners' letter on General Dampierre's death, and (needing framing) the War Office paragraph on the treaty commissioners at the Rapids of the Miami. Weaker: the Rome paragraph and the Paris 'sullen tranquillity' paragraph (digest paragraphs) and Captain Hacket's Amsterdam rumour (two wordings, 4 + 2).
not_admitted.Left out for framing: The German Creek letter on a raid on the 'valley Indian towns' (6 papers), Captain Fanning's account of the burning of Cap Francais (6), the brig Mary's report of the dead at Cap Francais (6), the civil commissioners' proclamation giving liberty to the 'negro warriors' (4), the Fugitive Slave Act (its text in 2 papers), the letter of Polverel and Sonthonax to Genet (4), the prosecutions of Singleterry and Henfield (5; private seamen) and a killing near Middletown, New Jersey (5; private people).
not_admitted.Below 6 papers: The Ostend news by the ship Fortitude (5), Jefferson's letter to the Philadelphia merchants on spoliations (5), Marat's funeral (5), the Convention's decree arresting foreigners (5, a digest paragraph), the revocation of vice-consul Duplaine's exequatur and Genet's answer (4 each), Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation of 9 April (5), Dumouriez's letter from Louvain (4), the ship William (5), and others listed in the README.

data_issues.Misdated issues: Two Gazette of the United States issues are filed under dates their mastheads contradict, confirmed on the scans: the issue filed under 4 April 1793 is Saturday 4 May (Whole No. 419), and the one filed under 23 July is Saturday 13 July (No. 439). No admitted printing is on them (masthead_dates.csv).
data_issues.A second scan filed under another date: Pages 3 and 4 filed under the American Herald of Liberty of 2 July 1793 are a second scan of the 9 July issue's pages 3 and 4 (page 3 prints 'BOSTON, JULY 3' and the 9 July heading). No admitted printing is on them (page_date_flags.csv).
data_issues.Misfiled RevX pages: Two 1793 issues have RevX transcriptions filed one page off (Kentucky Gazette 6 April, edition 2; the Mirrour, 22 April). No admitted printing is on them.
data_issues.The Kentucky Gazette of 1793: Its 1793 mastheads agree with the filed dates (all 67 front pages read, both copies counted: 64 agree, and the other 3 are misread or misprinted days), unlike the Kentucky Gazette and General Advertiser of 1806 to 1808. Most issues were scanned twice (editions 1 and 2).
